{"task": {"id": "I_kwDOVRCof88AAAABiXayqw", "item_id": "PVTI_lAHOAHSLSM4Bn7ElzhLuvrQ", "project_id": "PVT_kwHOAHSLSM4Bn7El", "number": 237, "title": "Persist IDE hard disks locally with crash-safe checkpoints and automatic startup restoration", "body": "## Goal

Persist the mounted PC-9821Ap IDE hard disk in browser-local storage so users can install a PC-98 game once, close the tab, and reopen the emulator with the installed game and saved files still present. This is HDD persistence, not a CPU/RAM save-state feature.

**Data safety and gameplay performance take priority over automatic saving.** Prefer automatic checkpointing when it can be implemented without material performance degradation. If that is not practical, a simple explicit **Save disk** action with automatic restoration on the next visit is an acceptable completed implementation of this Issue. Do not delay completion in pursuit of a perfect autosave system.

## Current implementation and useful entry points

- [web/app.js](https://github.com/takahirox/pc98-rust/blob/main/web/app.js): startup calls `defaultHdd({startup:true})`; HDD import uses bounded 1 MiB chunks and transactional `hdi_begin/append/commit/cancel`; `exportBlob(2)` pauses the guest and reads a consistent image through `snapshot/readChunk`. `mayReplace` uses `hdi_dirty_page` to protect modified media.
- [src/lib.rs](https://github.com/takahirox/pc98-rust/blob/main/src/lib.rs): existing `hdi_dirty_page`, `hdi_len`, and `hdi_read_chunk` exports are useful starting points. Inspect their semantics before reusing them for incremental persistence: an export-dirty page is not necessarily a page changed since the last durable checkpoint.
- [web/emulator-worker.js](https://github.com/takahirox/pc98-rust/blob/main/web/emulator-worker.js): the authoritative emulation Worker owns the mounted disk and media transactions. Keep that ownership; storage I/O should not block normal emulation.
- [web/index.html](https://github.com/takahirox/pc98-rust/blob/main/web/index.html): the current Help correctly says disk changes remain in memory; revise this for the new behavior. Keep the existing screen-first UI and IDE HDD picker.

## Implementation

### Persistence and startup

- Prefer **Origin Private File System (OPFS)** for large binary disk images, with a small transactional index/manifest as needed. IndexedDB or another browser-local storage approach is acceptable if it provides equivalent crash-safe behavior and measured performance. Do not put HDD bytes in localStorage.
- Persist both the bundled writable FreeDOS HDD after installation/modification and user-imported supported HDI/NHD disks, preserving the image format, exact byte length, content, and identifying metadata. Reuse bounded chunked I/O; avoid extra full-image RAM copies.
- On subsequent startup, restore the last successfully committed HDD before boot. If no saved HDD exists, use the existing FreeDOS startup path. A failed or corrupt saved image must not silently be replaced or erased by a fresh FreeDOS image; show a useful recovery option and preserve recoverable data.
- Keep Export disk for external backups and the existing per-drive media actions. Explicit replacement/eject/Restore FreeDOS must respect unsaved changes, confirmations, and the intended next startup disk; do not resurrect an intentionally ejected/replaced disk unexpectedly. Preserve the Ap HDD when temporarily switching to VM.
- Keep everything local to this browser/origin; no server upload, cloud storage, new network service, or proprietary test media.

### Crash-safe checkpoints

- Never modify the only known-good committed image in place without a safe recovery mechanism. Use a staged immutable generation, transactional dirty-page journal, or another justified copy-on-write/checkpoint scheme. Publish a new generation only after its necessary data is durably written and validated; retain at least the previous recoverable generation when committing changes. Bound old-generation/journal storage and clean up incomplete writes only when safe.
- Capture a coherent guest disk checkpoint at a defined Worker boundary. Writes arriving during a save must not disappear or be falsely marked committed. If using incremental checkpoints, track changes since the last successful commit and retain dirty state until acknowledgment.
- On interrupted save (tab closed/reloaded, Worker terminated, storage error), restore the last complete valid checkpoint or offer the previous generation, never a partially written mixture. Do not depend on asynchronous save work in beforeunload/pagehide completing.
- Prevent concurrent writers to the same persisted disk from multiple tabs (e.g. an exclusive origin-scoped lock); a second tab must not silently overwrite the first tab's data. On storage unavailable/quota error, keep the live disk and last committed generation intact and make recovery/export possible.
- Clarify that crash-safe host persistence does not make arbitrary DOS filesystem writes atomic: a checkpoint taken during an incomplete guest FAT/file update can still contain guest-level inconsistency. Keep a previous checkpoint as recovery and explain saving after the guest finishes writing. Browser storage may be cleared/evicted; backups remain important.

### Performance and UX

- Prefer periodic **dirty-only** checkpoints while the guest is running, with no writes when unchanged. Use bounded transferable chunks, asynchronous storage or a dedicated storage Worker if appropriate, and avoid full-disk hashing/scanning/copying on every timer tick. Do not run blocking storage I/O on the emulator Worker or AudioWorklet; bound producer-side work and avoid unbounded queues.
- Measure normal release-Wasm gameplay with BGM before and during saving on the same representative rights-cleared workload. Check guest/wall time, presentation FPS and audio underflow/drop counts, and save cost. Do not accept a material repeatable gameplay slowdown or newly introduced audio gaps, alter emulated timing, or increase audio latency to mask the cost.
- **If safe background autosave is too expensive or complex, ship explicit manual Save disk instead.** Place it in the existing IDE HDD Change/actions picker, distinct from Export disk. A deliberate manual save may pause emulation briefly with progress, then resume the previous state; no periodic heavy work is required. Users must not have to manually import the saved image next time. For autosave, a compact indication of pending/saving/saved/error state is sufficient; avoid extra permanent controls or dialogs. Clearly indicate the last successful save and unsaved changes when relevant.

## Mandatory acceptance (bounded scope)

1. Install/copy a test application or file onto the bundled HDD and modify a user-imported HDD in the actual browser runtime; commit via autosave or Save disk. Reload/reopen and boot the correct saved image automatically, with exact committed changes intact and no reinstall.
2. Demonstrate interruption during a staged save and a storage failure: the previous committed image remains valid, the partial save is not selected, and a subsequent save can succeed. Verify recovery from a bad latest checkpoint, concurrent-tab write protection, and explicit replacement/restore/cancel behavior. Use targeted deterministic storage tests plus representative real browser reload coverage; no exhaustive browser/race permutation matrix.
3. Preserve existing boot, media import/export, dirty-disk safeguards, UI, Pointer Lock, CRT and audio behavior. Provide a representative before/after performance comparison; select manual save if automatic saving causes material regressions.
4. Pass applicable existing required checks, focused storage/browser regressions and publication/security checks for both serving roots. Update Help/README with the actual save policy, limitations, recovery and backup workflow.

**Completion boundary:** a reliable manual Save disk + automatic startup restoration satisfies the core requirement if automatic saving would compromise performance or significantly expand implementation scope. A complete disk library, multiple saved-disk profiles, save states, floppy persistence, exhaustive crash permutations, and perfect guest filesystem crash recovery are not required. Record nonblocking limitations; do not repeatedly extend review scope or rerun identical successful suites. Preserve required protections and fix genuine data-loss or major ordinary-use defects before merge.

Related: #127 (large HDD I/O), #130 (FreeDOS), #233/#235 (current player UI), #146 (performance).

## Required post-merge verification
